Chapter 4: The Struggle Within—Internalized Oppression and Community Tensions
Sometimes, the toughest battles aren’t the ones you see coming from outside—they’re the ones we wrestle with inside ourselves. For Black women, the weight of racism and sexism doesn’t just come from the world around them—it can sneak into the way they see themselves, and even into their relationships with each other.
It’s almost like the world’s messages seep in, planting seeds of doubt, fear, and even resentment. And these feelings? They don’t just show up out of nowhere. They’re shaped by the world, then become part of the stories we tell ourselves.
In so many Black communities, survival has always depended on unity. Families, neighbors—they look out for each other, sharing what little they have. There’s a real strength in that togetherness, but it can also bring pressure. Women, especially, often feel expected to put everyone else’s needs before their own, sometimes sacrificing their dreams just to keep the group strong.
Picture this: a daughter watches her mother work herself to the bone, never complaining, always giving. She grows up believing that her own needs have to come last. And if she dares to speak up for herself? She risks being called selfish or ungrateful. The message is loud and clear—being strong means staying silent.
Now, here’s something most people don’t notice—the wounds of racism can make it even harder to talk about sexism. There’s a real fear that bringing up these issues might divide the community, or hand outsiders more reasons to judge. Some worry that challenging men’s behavior will weaken the fight for racial justice. So, what happens? A heavy silence settles in. Everyone knows there’s a problem, but no one feels safe enough to name it.
This silence? It can turn into resentment. Women may feel invisible, their hard work taken for granted. Men, too, are shaped by history—expected to lead and protect, but not always encouraged to be equals. The pressure to be strong and always in control makes it tough to show vulnerability or admit mistakes.
Think about how this plays out in everyday life. A woman might hesitate to take a new job, worried about leaving her family behind. Or a friend might struggle to talk about her relationship, afraid she’ll be judged. These aren’t just personal struggles—they’re the echoes of centuries of oppression, passed down through generations.
And yet, even with all these challenges, there are bright spots—real moments of hope. Imagine a group of friends gathered in someone’s kitchen, sharing stories, laughter, and finding strength together. Or a mother telling her daughter to dream big, to believe she truly deserves more. These small, everyday acts of support? They’re the seeds of real change.
What becomes clear is that true liberation takes more than new laws or policies. It means healing those wounds inside—learning to see ourselves, and each other, as worthy of love, respect, and freedom.
